'''Aram Wettroth Harrow''' (born 1980) is an American [[Quantum information science|quantum information scientist]]. He has been a professor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] since 2013.<ref name="homepage">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mit.edu/~aram/|title=Aram Harrow|website=www.mit.edu|access-date=2018-02-21}}</ref>

He was born on April 22, 1980 in [[Lansing, Michigan]]<ref name="i794">{{cite journal |date=August 2008 |title=Contributors |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/ielx5/18/27300/01214090.pdf |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=49 |issue=8 |publisher=IEEE Information Theory Society |pages=2077–2080 }}</ref> to a family descended from Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe<ref name="z468">{{cite book | last=Harrow | first=Kenneth W. | title=Space and Time in African Cinema and Cine-Scapes | date=2022 | isbn=978-1-032-26570-4 | page=x}}</ref><ref name="k347">{{Cite web |last=Saba |first=Alix |date=2024-04-16 |title=Kenneth W. Harrow (1943-2024) |url=https://africanstudies.org/in-memory/kenneth-w-harrow-1943-2024/ |website=African Studies Association Portal - ASA |language=en-US}}</ref> and attended high school in [[East Lansing]].<ref name="x316">{{cite web | title=Physics honors students with awards | website=MIT News | date=2001-06-06 | url=https://news.mit.edu/2001/physics-0606 }}</ref> In 2001, he received an SB from MIT and completed an undergraduate thesis in the [[MIT Media Lab]] advised by [[Neil Gershenfeld]], also working closely with Benjamin Recht, a graduate student of Gershenfeld's.<ref name="a001">{{cite web | title=Quantum Compiling |last=Harrow |first=Aram  | website=MIT | date=2001-05-18 | url=http://www.cba.mit.edu/docs/theses/01.05.aram.pdf |url-status=live  | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130403125632/http://www.cba.mit.edu/docs/theses/01.05.aram.pdf | archive-date=2013-04-03 }}</ref>

In 2005, he received a PhD advised by MIT electrical engineering professor [[Isaac Chuang]]. From 2005 to 2010 he was a lecturer at the [[University of Bristol]], and from 2010 to 2012 he was a postdoctoral researcher at the [[University of Washington]].<ref name="homepage" /> He joined MIT in 2013.

In 2008, Harrow, Avinatan Hassidim, and [[Seth Lloyd]] introduced the [[HHL algorithm]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Harrow|first1=Aram W.|last2=Hassidim|first2=Avinatan|last3=Lloyd|first3=Seth|author-link3=Seth Lloyd|date=2009-10-07|title=Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations|journal=[[Physical Review Letters]]|volume=103|issue=15|article-number=150502|arxiv=0811.3171|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.150502|pmid=19905613|bibcode=2009PhRvL.103o0502H|s2cid=5187993 }}</ref> The algorithm was widely thought to give [[quantum machine learning]] algorithms with exponential speedups over the best classical algorithms, until the discovery by [[Ewin Tang]] of classical algorithms giving the same exponential speedups.<ref name="Tang18b">{{Cite journal|last=Tang|first=Ewin|title=Quantum Principal Component Analysis Only Achieves an Exponential Speedup Because of Its State Preparation Assumptions|journal=Physical Review Letters|year=2021|volume=127|issue=6|article-number=060503|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.127.060503|pmid=34420330|arxiv=1811.00414|bibcode=2021PhRvL.127f0503T|s2cid=236956378}}</ref> Harrow later attempted to propose an alternative approach to quantum machine learning, although it did not become as widespread as the HHL algorithm.<ref name="i218">{{cite arXiv | last=Harrow | first=Aram W. | title=Small quantum computers and large classical data sets  | date=2020-03-31 | class=quant-ph | eprint=2004.00026 }}</ref>

In 2015, Harrow and Lior Eldar, a postdoctoral researcher at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]], announced a solution to the [[NLTS conjecture]] of [[Michael Freedman]] and [[Matthew Hastings]],<ref name="t632">{{cite arXiv | last1=Eldar | first1=Lior | last2=Harrow | first2=Aram W. | title=Local Hamiltonians with No Low-energy Trivial States | date=2015-10-07 | class=quant-ph | eprint=1510.02082v2 }}</ref> which was later modified to prove the weaker NLETS theorem after a mistake was discovered.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Eldar |first=Lior |date=2017 |title=Local Hamiltonians Whose Ground States are Hard to Approximate |url=http://ieee-focs.org/FOCS-2017-Papers/3464a427.pdf |access-date=Aug 7, 2022 |website=IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)}}</ref> A proof of the original NLTS conjecture was eventually given in 2023 by Anurag Anshu, [[Nikolas Breuckmann]], and Chinmay Nirkhe.

He is on the steering committee of Quantum Information Processing (QIP), an annual [[quantum computing]] conference.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://qipconference.org/|title=Home|website=qipconference.org|language=en-gb|access-date=2018-02-21}}</ref> He is the creator and co-administrator of SciRate, a [[Reddit]]-inspired website for voting and commenting on papers which have been submitted to [[arXiv]].<ref name="Scirate">{{cite web |url=https://scirate.com/about|title=Top arXiv papers|website=SciRate|language=en-US}}</ref>

His father was [[Kenneth W. Harrow]], an English professor at [[Michigan State University]] known for his contributions to African literature.<ref name="z468" /> He is married to Shefali Oza, an epidemiology researcher at Harvard.<ref name="z468" />
